meta.title: Claude Haiku 5.5 · Materials science · solo · run 2
meta.note: Main run, 60 minutes. The verifier accepted 3 of 10 credited claims; 2 set a new best held-out result on their dataset. Verdicts from the re-run of the official verifier.

artifacts.title: LightGBM on extended Magpie-style composition features beats the HGB baseline on experimental band gaps (5-fold CV MAE)
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0458, 95% CI [-0.0624, -0.0284], beyond the minimum effect 0.0083)

claim.statement: On expt_gap (Matbench experimental band gaps, 3440 train rows), a LightGBM regressor (1500 trees, lr 0.02, 31 leaves, colsample 0.6, subsample 0.8) on fraction-weighted mean/std/min/max/range of 20+ elemental properties plus composition entropy and fraction statistics reaches 5-fold CV MAE 0.422 eV, versus 0.476 eV for the reference HistGradientBoosting baseline under the same folds. Predictions are clipped at zero.

artifacts.title: LightGBM on extended Magpie-style composition features beats the HGB baseline on experimental metallicity classification (5-fold CV error)

events.text: I need to learn how the lab works before choosing a problem, so I'll read the guide and the command list first.
The guide is clear. Next I'll look at the datasets, their READMEs, and the baselines the evaluator compares against, so I can pick a problem where a real improvement is possible.
Before choosing a target I need to see what the evaluator's baseline does and how it scores, so I'll read the baseline script and the dataset metadata.

The baseline is a plain Magpie-lite HistGradientBoosting model, so there's room to improve. I'll check which ML libraries are installed and get the baseline CV numbers for `expt_gap` and `expt_is_metal` as reference points.

Band gap regression (`expt_gap`, baseline CV MAE 0.476 eV) has the most room to improve. I'll write a script that reproduces the baseline, then compares an extended Magpie-style featurizer with LightGBM and ExtraTrees, plus their ensemble. Predictions are clipped at zero because gaps are non-negative.

The first run shows LightGBM alone at 0.422 CV MAE, slightly better than the 0.424 ensemble and well below the baseline's 0.476. I'll make the prediction path use LightGBM alone, check it on a fake held-out file, then record the CV comparison through `lab exec`.

```bash
cd /tmp/exp1 && python - <<'EOF'
s = open("run.py").read()
s = s.replace('pred = np.clip(0.5 * p["lgbm"] + 0.5 * p["et"], 0, None)', 'pred = np.clip(p["lgbm"], 0, None)')
s = s.replace('    p = run_all(X, y, Xt, None, None)\n', '    p = {"lgbm": lgbm(X, y, Xt)}\n')
open("run.py", "w").write(s)
EOF
mkdir -p /tmp/fake/expt_gap &

The exec ran in prediction mode and failed, so `EVAL_DIR` seems to be set inside `lab exec` even without a test directory. I'll make the script choose its mode by whether an inputs file exists, then rerun the CV measurement through `lab exec`.

```bash
cd /tmp/exp1 && python - <<'EOF'
s = open("run.py").read()
s = s.replace('EVAL = os.environ.get("EVAL_DIR")', 'EVAL = os.environ.get("EVAL_DIR")\nimport glob as _g\nif EVAL is not None and not _g.glob(f"{EVAL}/expt_gap/inputs.*"):\n    EVAL = None')
open("run.py", "w").write(s)
EOF
lab exec /tmp/exp1 -- env DATA_DIR=/lab/data python run.py
```

The CV run is recorded as `exec-af461e31`, with LightGBM at 0.422 MAE against the baseline's 0.476. I'll publish that as a finding, with a prediction test that uses the same code and command.

```bash
cd /tmp/exp1 && cat > f1.json <<'EOF'
{"kind": "finding",
 "title": "LightGBM on extended Magpie-style composition features beats the HGB baseline on experimental band gaps (5-fold CV MAE)",
 "claim": {"statement": "On expt_gap (Matbench experimental band gaps, 3440 train rows), a LightGBM regressor (1500 trees, lr 0.02, 31 leaves, colsample 0.6, subsample 0.8) on fraction-weighted mean/std/min/m

The prediction test is set up for the band-gap finding. Next I'll check whether the same feature set and LightGBM help on the metallic-classification task, where the baseline error is 0.0906. The script runs CV and writes predictions in the same way.

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/exp2 && cp /lab/data/baselines/materials_baseline.py /tmp/exp2/ && cat > /tmp/exp2/run.py <<'EOF'
import os, sys, glob, json
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
from materials_baseline import parse_formula, baseline_predict
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold

The metal classifier also beats the baseline: LightGBM reaches 0.0779 CV error against 0.0906 for the reference model, recorded as `exec-e46a230a`. I'll publish it as a finding with a prediction test that uses the same code.

```bash
cd /tmp/exp2 && cat > f2.json <<'EOF'
{"kind": "finding",
 "title": "LightGBM on extended Magpie-style composition features beats the HGB baseline on experimental metallicity classification (5-fold CV error)",
 "claim": {"statement": "On expt_is_metal (Matbench, 3685 train rows), a LightGBM classifier (1000 trees, lr 0.02, 31 leaves, colsample 0.6, subsample 0.8)

Both findings are recorded. Next I'll test the same featurizer and LightGBM on `glass` (classification) and `steels` (regression, 237 rows), since those may also have room over the baseline. I'll run the baseline and LightGBM under identical 5-fold CV for each.


```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/exp3 && cp /lab/data/baselines/materials_baseline.py /tmp/exp3/ && cat > /tmp/exp3/run.py <<'EOF'
import os, sys, glob, json
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
from materials_baseline import parse_formula, baseline_predict
from sklearn.model_selection i

Both new results beat the baseline. Steels improves by about 9% (MAE 134.9 to 122.4 MPa) and glass by about 6% (error 0.1173 to 0.1108). I'll publish both as findings with prediction tests. Each test reuses the same script, with `DS_NAME` set in the command for the dataset.

```bash
cd /tmp/exp3 && cat > f3.json <<'EOF'
{"kind": "finding",
 "title": "LightGBM on Magpie-style composition features beats the HGB baseline on Citrine steel yield strength (5-fold CV MAE)",
 "claim": {"statement": "On steels (Matbench/Citrine yield strength, 237 rows), a LightGBM regressor (1500 trees, lr 0.02, 31 le

Both findings passed live checks. The band-gap finding has the largest margin, so I'll try to extend it. I'll add a per-element fraction vector to the features, which often helps on Matbench composition tasks, and check whether CV improves over the current LightGBM.

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/exp4 && cp /lab/data/baselines/materials_baseline.py /tmp/exp4/ && cat > /tmp/exp4/run.py <<'EOF'
import os, sys, glob, json
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
from materials_baseline import parse_formula
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
im

The fraction vector cut CV MAE by only 0.0025 eV (about 0.6%), which is too small to claim as a meaningful improvement, so I won't publish it. I'll try one more batch of expt_gap variants: a Huber loss, a log-transformed target, and a deeper model. I'll compare them against the current LightGBM under the same folds.

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/exp5 && cp /lab/data/baselines/materials_baseline.py /tmp/exp5/ && cat > /tmp/exp5/run.py <<'EOF'
import os, sys, glob, json
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
from materials_baseline import parse_f

The log-target variant scores 0.406 MAE against 0.422 for the base model, a 3.7% gain. Since I picked it from four variants on the same folds, I'll first check that it holds under two different fold splits before publishing.

```bash
cd /tmp/exp5 && python - <<'EOF'
s = open("run.py").read()
s = s.replace('VARIANTS = ["base", "huber", "logy", "deep"]', 'VARIANTS = ["base", "logy"]\nKSEED = int(os.environ.get("KSEED", "0"))')
s = s.replace('KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)', 'KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=KSEED)')
open("run.py", "w").write(s)
EOF
lab exec /tmp/exp5 -- env DATA_DIR=/

The log-target variant holds up across three fold seeds: 0.406, 0.403 and 0.399 MAE, against 0.422, 0.423 and 0.418 for the base model. That is a consistent gain of about 0.02 eV, so I'll publish it. First I'll check that the prediction path runs with `VARIANT=logy`, since the evaluator will run that command.

```bash
cd /tmp/exp5 && DATA_DIR=/lab/data EVAL_DIR=/tmp/fake OUT_DIR=/tmp/fake_out5 VARIANT=logy python run.py && head -3 /tmp/fake_out5/predictions.csv && wc -l /tmp/fake_out5/predictions.csv
cat > f5.json <<'EOF'
{"kind": "finding",
 "title": "Fitting LightGBM on log(1+gap) improves e

The contribution failed a live check: the baseline number comes from `exec-af461e31`, which I didn't list as evidence. I'll rerun seed 0 under the current script so every quantity comes from the same code version, then resubmit with all the supporting execs listed.

```bash
cd /tmp/exp5 && lab exec /tmp/exp5 -- env DATA_DIR=/lab/data KSEED=0 python run.py
```

The new run gives the same seed-0 numbers (0.4064 for log-target, 0.4219 for base). I'll resubmit with `exec-af461e31` added as evidence for the baseline number, and point the test at the current code hash, which matches the run that produced these metrics.

```bash
cd /tmp/exp5 && cat > f5b.json <<'EOF'
{"kind": "finding",
 "title": "Fitting LightGBM on log(1+gap) improves expt_gap band-gap regression over the base LightGBM across three CV fold seeds",
 "claim": {"statement": "On expt_gap, a LightGBM regressor trained on log1p(band gap) with predictions mapped back by expm1 and clipped at zer

The band-gap finding is published and passed live checks. Next I'll check whether the two smaller margins hold up. Glass improved by only 0.0065, and steels has no seed check yet. I'll rerun both across fold seeds 1 and 2 in a fresh copy of the script, with a log-target variant for steels.

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/exp6 && cp /lab/data/baselines/materials_baseline.py /tmp/exp6/ && cat > /tmp/exp6/run.py <<'EOF'
import os, sys, glob, json
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
from materials_baseline import parse_formula, baseline_predict
fr

Glass replicates: LightGBM beats the baseline at all three fold seeds, by 0.008 to 0.009. Steels also beats the baseline at all three seeds, but the log-target variant is mixed there (it wins at seed 0 and loses at seed 1), so I won't claim it for steels. I'll publish a glass finding that cites all three seed runs, after checking that the prediction path of the glass script runs.

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/fake/glass && python -c "
import pandas as pd; tr=pd.read_csv('/lab/data/glass/train.csv'); tr.sample(200,random_state=2)[['id','composition']].to_csv('/tmp/fake/glass/inputs.csv',index=False)"

The glass replicate passed live checks. Steels improved over the baseline at all three seeds with the base LightGBM (the log-target variant was mixed, so I'm leaving it out). Next I'll check the steels prediction path and run the metal classifier at two more fold seeds, which tests whether its earlier margin holds.

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/fake/steels && python -c "
import pandas as pd; tr=pd.read_csv('/lab/data/steels/train.csv'); tr.sample(50,random_state=3)[['id','composition']].to_csv('/tmp/fake/steels/inputs.csv',index=False)"
cd /tmp/exp6 && DATA_DIR=/lab/data DS_NAME=steels EVAL_DIR=/tmp/

Both replicate runs for the metal classifier beat the baseline (0.0798 vs 0.0898 at seed 1, 0.0776 vs 0.0896 at seed 2). I'll check the metal prediction path on fake inputs, since neither metal finding has had that check yet. Then I'll publish the steels finding and the metal replicate.

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/fake/expt_is_metal && python -c "
import pandas as pd; tr=pd.read_csv('/lab/data/expt_is_metal/train.csv'); tr.sample(200,random_state=4)[['id','composition']].to_csv('/tmp/fake/expt_is_metal/inputs.csv',index=False)"
cd /tmp/exp6 && DATA_DIR=/lab/data DS_NAME=expt_is_metal EVAL_DIR=/tmp/

The metal finding failed a live check because I included the glass number, which comes from a different exec that I didn't cite. I'll resubmit with only the metal quantities and their own evidence.

```bash
cd /tmp/exp6 && python - <<'EOF'
import json
f = json.load(open("/dev/stdin")) if False else None
EOF
cat > f8b.json <<'EOF'
{"kind": "finding",
 "title": "LightGBM on Magpie-style composition features beats the HGB baseline on experimental metallicity classification across three CV fold seeds",
 "claim": {"statement": "On expt_is_metal (Matbench, 3685 rows), a LightGBM classifier on fracti
Run the log-target LightGBM, the log-target ExtraTrees, and their average under fold seeds 0, 1 and 2. Only one experiment, so the comparison stays clean. Record all metrics in one exec.
Rerun the same CV folds, but compute the 50/50 blend of log-target LightGBM and ExtraTrees on each fold and record its MAE. I'll also record the blend weights so the claim matches the code.
Same experiment as before, with only the import path fixed so the module loads from the exec's working directory.
Post a short summary of what was negative so other researchers don't repeat it, then end my part of the session.

Negative results (expt_gap): (1) adding per-element fraction vector to LightGBM features: -0.0025 eV CV MAE, too small to claim. (2) Huber loss and deeper LightGBM (63 leaves): no gain over base. (3) 50/50 blend of log-target LightGBM and log-target ExtraTrees is worse than LightGBM alone at all three fold seeds (0.410/0.410/0.404 vs 0.406/0.403/0.399). Log-target LightGBM gain holds at seeds 0-2. Steels log-target is mixed across seeds, not claimed. Published: expt_gap logy (findin-e91419eb), glass (findin-08f23167), steels (findin-? see artifacts), expt_is_metal (findin-514b121c and earlier findin-a870a739).
